t: About me
x: About me Hi 👋 This page is a short manual for working with me. It's for colleagues, teammates and anyone I'm starting something with: so we spend less time getting used to each other and more time on the product . What I do By day I'm a product manager, and as a PhD student at RANEPA I'm writing a dissertation on “Using artificial intelligence to improve a company's management system” . It's the same topic from two sides: at work I build a service with an AI agent for credit analysis, and in my research I look at how AI changes not individual tasks but management itself — planning, decision-making, control and communication inside a company. I'm interested in three questions: in which management processes AI really makes a difference, and where it's just hype; what risks and limitations it brings — from data quality to accountability for a decision; what a company needs to prepare in advance: data, infrastructure, people and rules. That's what my articles and talks are about, and I cover the practical side in the AI agents section. What I believe in Hypothesis → test → decision One primary metric per experiment Business results matter more than the number of features AI strengthens management but doesn't take responsibility away from people Process and data first, the model second AI where it delivers measurable value, not AI for its own sake How to work with me I start with “why”. Before discussing a solution, I'll ask which user or business problem we're solving and how we'll know we've solved it. It's not distrust, it's a habit. I like numbers and facts. An opinion without data is a fine starting point, but I want to make decisions based on customer interviews, analytics or an experiment. Sober about AI. If you suggest “adding AI”, I'll ask which process it will improve, how we'll measure the effect and who is responsible when the model is wrong. If there are answers, I'm the first to support it. Feedback — directly. If something is wrong with the product, the process or my work, tell me right away and to the point. I give feedback the same way: specifically, with a suggestion for what to change. Bad news — early. A missed deadline I learn about a week ahead is plan B. The same deadline I learn about on release day is a fire. Communication. I reply fastest on Telegram. I read email, but not instantly. If it's urgent, say so. Meetings. A meeting needs a goal and an outcome: at the end we write down who does what and by when. If you're unsure whether to message me — message me. t: What holds AI back in management — findings from interviews at a large bank
x: What holds AI back in management — findings from interviews at a large bank For the empirical part of my PhD I ran a series of semi-structured interviews inside a large Russian bank. The question is simple: how does AI actually get built into a company's management system — and what gets in the way? Below are generalised findings, without the bank's name, people's names or internal figures. The case Object. A large Russian bank with a wide branch network, moving from isolated pilots to systematic use of AI. Who I interviewed. Four groups of respondents: product and project managers who implement AI initiatives; specialists from the AI technology centre; top management; employees who use AI tools in their work. How. One interview guide: a common block for everyone and a specialised block per role. Interviews are anonymised, key quotes extracted, answers coded into a thematic matrix — which themes repeat across groups. How AI is governed A dedicated structure above departments. There's an AI centre with its own strategy and a data management function next to it. Strategic goals and adoption KPIs are set at the top and cascade down to department heads. Initiatives come from the business. A unit brings a problem; together with the AI centre it's turned into an AI task with a target metric. Business units have "AI advocates" — people who know the processes and understand what AI can and can't do. Selection by three criteria: economic effect, data readiness and process repeatability. If the effect is large but the data isn't ready, the initiative becomes "preparatory": fix data and processes first, then pilot. Accountability stays with the business. If AI scoring is built into the lending process, the risk manager owns the decision. AI is a tool, not the accountable party. Where AI already works Maturity differs a lot by area. Classic machine learning has long been in production: anti-fraud, scoring, speech analytics in the contact centre. Generative AI is moving from pilots to scale: internal assistants for staff, document summarisation, drafts of analytical reports. Agentic systems are at an early pilot stage. Five barriers Process, not the model. The most common answer: the blocker isn't model accuracy but the lack of a business process where the output becomes a step rather than "one more dashboard for reference". It's an organisational problem, and it's slow to fix because it touches people's areas of responsibility. Data. In a pilot the data is pulled by hand; production needs an automated pipeline — and it turns out sources update at the wrong frequency and have no availability guarantees. People and trust. Employees either blindly trust the model's suggestion — making its error their error — or ignore it. A tool can be technically available for months while only a small share of staff use it. Plus a shortage of specialists and dependence on a few experts. Line managers. Adoption hinges on line managers: if they don't understand what AI can and can't do, "pseudo-AI" initiatives appear and real opportunities are missed. Regulation and security. Customers' personal data rules out external models — you need a closed environment, which limits model choice. Final decisions need explainability and a fallback: why the model decided this and how to challenge it. Models drift with the portfolio and the economy and need constant monitoring. Takeaways Autonomous AI-based management decisions are unacceptable in a bank today. The model is an adviser: it collects and structures information, highlights risks, double-checks data. The decision stays with a human. A gap between the model and the decision is normal, not a failure. The model optimises one objective; a management decision balances several, some of which can't be formalised. Start narrow. An example from the interviews: instead of a churn model for the whole portfolio, it was launched for one segment and one channel where data and a retention process already existed. A smaller but measurable and fast effect — and the right to scale. If you change one thing — build AI literacy into line managers' planning and create a single platform of reusable components so a new initiative launches in weeks, not months. What it means for a product manager Almost all barriers are product problems, not technical ones: which process the output plugs into, who owns it, how users know when to trust the model, which metric defines success. I follow the same principles building a service with an AI agent at work and in my own AI projects . More about the PhD on the research page. I wrote about AI risks in banks in an article and a talk .

t: "Inspired" by Marty Cagan: the essentials of product management
x: "Inspired" by Marty Cagan: the essentials of product management 10 /10 — my rating Key ideas from the core book on the product manager's job: how strong product teams differ from "feature factories" and why most ideas don't work the first time. Marty Cagan is a former product leader at eBay, Netscape and HP and the founder of Silicon Valley Product Group. "Inspired" is his book on how technology companies create products customers love. Below is what I took from it and use at work and in my course. Most ideas won't work The book's main idea: at least half of our ideas won't deliver, and those that do will need several iterations. So a strong team doesn't "deliver the roadmap" — it quickly and cheaply filters out bad ideas before engineering time is spent on them. Four risks Before building, the team tests four risks: Value — will people buy it or use it? Usability — can users figure out how to use it? Feasibility — can we build it in reasonable time and budget? Business viability — does it work for the business: legal, sales, finance, brand? The product manager owns value and viability, the designer usability, the tech lead feasibility. Discovery and Delivery A product team works on two parallel tracks. Discovery — figuring out what's worth building: interviews, prototypes, quick experiments. Delivery — building it well and shipping. Many companies only do the second. I gave this pair its own slide in the first lecture of my IT management course. Prototypes instead of specs Instead of long requirements, Cagan suggests testing ideas with prototypes: from a clickable mockup to a "Wizard of Oz", where a human works behind the interface by hand. A prototype costs days, not months, and answers "do we need this?" before development. Missionaries, not mercenaries A mercenary team does what it's told. A missionary team gets a problem and owns the outcome — that the solution works, not just that it shipped. For that, the team needs context: product vision, strategy and clear goals. Who the product manager is For Cagan, the PM owns the product's value and viability, and needs deep knowledge of four things: users, data, the business, and the market and industry. Not a "backlog owner" or project manager — the person who decides what's worth building. Who should read it Anyone working in product or planning to. For beginners it's a map of the profession; for experienced PMs, the language to explain to the business why a product team shouldn't be a feature factory. If you read one book on product management, read this one.

t: bolz.dev — an MCP connector that lets AI agents take real-world actions
x: bolz.dev — an MCP connector that lets AI agents take real-world actions In August 2025 we built the MVP of bolz.dev — a Model Context Protocol platform that lets AI agents not just recommend but finish the job: find, book and pay for real services. The problem Agents are great at search but almost always end by sending the user to a website link — "take it from here". The best models complete real-world tasks less than half the time (MCP-Universe benchmark). Buying a flight via an AI agent today takes longer than doing it yourself: the agent imitates a human — search, links, forms. On the other side are services: most companies risk not appearing in agent answers at all and losing customers. The solution Bolz Connector sits between agents and services: a service connects once — via a plugin, web interface or REST API; the agent gets normalised data, live prices and functions "search / reserve / confirm / refund / pay"; the user goes from request to payment to done in a single conversation. We designed two scenarios: a marketplace ("find a housewarming gift under $100") and taxi ("call a Comfort car and avoid traffic"). How to measure quality The key lesson: for such an agent, judging the model's answer isn't enough. Success is a completed action: a paid order, a car on its way, a purchased ticket. So we built in execution-based evals — checking the outcome, not the text. Why it matters to me bolz.dev grew out of bolz.tech, our sharing ecosystem: we saw users increasingly arrive via AI assistants rather than apps. For me it's also the most direct experience in the agent layer: MCP, agent tools, evals and metrics for agentic scenarios. I later applied the same approach in the Weekend Planner . t: Blue Ocean Strategy by Kim and Mauborgne: how to escape competition
x: Blue Ocean Strategy by Kim and Mauborgne: how to escape competition Key ideas from the book about not fighting competitors over an existing market but creating new market space where there is no competition yet. W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne are professors at INSEAD. The book is based on a study of strategic moves by companies across industries over more than a hundred years. Red and blue oceans A red ocean is an existing market with known rules where companies take share from each other. The more players, the lower the profits. A blue ocean is a market that doesn't exist yet. Demand is created rather than fought over. Value innovation The main idea is not to choose between differentiation and low cost but to pursue both. That's possible if you drop what the industry considers essential but customers don't need. The strategy canvas and four actions The strategy canvas shows the factors an industry competes on and the level each player offers. To draw a new value curve, the authors propose four questions: Eliminate — which factors the industry takes for granted should be eliminated? Reduce — what can be reduced well below the industry standard? Raise — what should be raised well above the standard? Create — what should be created that the industry has never offered? The classic example is Cirque du Soleil: a circus without animal acts and star performers, but with a storyline and artistic production, like theatre. Noncustomers New markets usually hide among noncustomers: those about to leave, those who consciously refuse the industry, and those who've never considered it. The question isn't "how do we win customers from competitors" but "why do these people use no one at all". What a PM can take from it Draw the strategy canvas for your category and go through the four questions: often the most valuable decision is to remove what all competitors do out of habit. Who should read it PMs and leaders stuck in a feature race with competitors. The book gives simple tools for a strategy session with the team.

t: Zero to One by Peter Thiel: how to build something truly new
x: Zero to One by Peter Thiel: how to build something truly new Key ideas from the PayPal co-founder's book on startups: why copying doesn't create the future, why aim for a monopoly, and which questions to ask yourself before starting. Peter Thiel co-founded PayPal and Palantir and was Facebook's first outside investor. The book grew out of his Stanford class, notes from which were taken by Blake Masters, the co-author. Zero to one or one to n Scaling what already works is going "from one to n". Creating something that didn't exist is going "from zero to one". Thiel argues that real progress comes only from the latter. The contrarian question "What important truth do very few people agree with you on?" A good answer is the basis of a company that sees an opportunity others missed. Competition is for losers Under intense competition, profits go to zero. The goal is to build a monopoly in your segment. Its features: proprietary technology at least 10 times better than alternatives; network effects — the product becomes more valuable with every user; economies of scale ; a strong brand . Start with a small market you can dominate completely, then expand. Sales matter as much as product Many engineers believe a good product sells itself. Thiel insists distribution is part of the product, and without a well-thought-out channel even the best solution won't take off. Seven questions for a startup Engineering, timing, monopoly, people, distribution, durability and the secret — the team needs a good answer to each. What a PM can take from it Before launch, check: in what way is our product many times better, not a few percent; in which small market can we become first; and how exactly will the product reach users. Who should read it Founders and PMs launching something new. The book is polemical — it's worth reading while arguing with the author.

t: Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman: how we get decisions wrong
x: Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman: how we get decisions wrong Key ideas from the Nobel laureate's book on the two systems of thinking and the systematic errors everyone makes — including in product decisions. Daniel Kahneman was a psychologist and winner of the Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on decision-making under uncertainty. The book brings together decades of research he did with Amos Tversky. Two systems System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless: it recognises faces, completes phrases, produces first impressions. System 2 is slow and effortful: it calculates, compares, checks. It's lazy and often just endorses what System 1 suggested. Errors worth knowing Anchoring. The first number you hear affects your estimate, even if it's random. Availability. We judge as likely what comes to mind easily: vivid, recent, loud. What you see is all there is. The mind builds a coherent story from the facts at hand and doesn't notice what's missing. Planning fallacy. We estimate time and cost from the best-case scenario. The cure is the "outside view": compare with similar projects instead of only analysing your own. Loss aversion. A loss feels stronger than an equal gain — the basis of prospect theory. Overconfidence. An expert's confidence reflects the coherence of their story, not the accuracy of the forecast. Two selves The "experiencing self" lives in the moment; the "remembering self" judges an experience by its peak and its end. So the impression of a service depends most on its most intense moment and how it ended. What a PM can take from it Estimate timelines through similar projects, not just the plan. Run a premortem before launch: imagine the project failed and write down why. Kahneman cites this technique from psychologist Gary Klein. Remember the peak and the end in the user journey: the last screen of a scenario matters more than it seems. Who should read it Anyone who makes decisions based on data and other people's opinions. The book is long — it's easiest to read in parts, returning to the chapters on biases.

t: My HSE master's thesis — how to tell whether digital transformation will pay off
x: My HSE master's thesis — how to tell whether digital transformation will pay off My master's thesis in the Corporate Finance programme at HSE University's Faculty of Economic Sciences was "Modelling and evaluating the efficiency of a company's digital transformation investment projects". It started the research line I now continue in my PhD at RANEPA — this time about AI. The problem Large companies invest huge sums in digital transformation, yet there are hardly any methods to forecast a project's success and estimate future benefits upfront. Existing evaluations: rely on qualitative criteria without clear ways to measure them; count only financial indicators and don't split capital and operating costs by technology area; report final effects without a calculation method, so the same indicators differ between sources. What I studied Analysed the digital transformation programmes of Rosseti ("Digital Transformation 2030"), Russian Railways ("Digital Railway") and Lukoil ("Digital Lukoil") and compared their technology bets: IoT, AI, big data, digital twins, robots and drones. Separated two concepts: digital optimisation improves existing processes, while digital transformation changes the value proposition and creates new products. Compared groups of evaluation methods — from cost accounting (TCO) to the balanced scorecard — and proposed steps for defining a project's non-financial metrics. Built a forecasting evaluation model with elements of risk scenario analysis. Four hypotheses Digital transformation projects are innovation projects and must be evaluated differently from ordinary investments: goals, timelines and costs are not fixed upfront. A company with steady growth can keep its competitive advantages for a while even without digital transformation. With outdated infrastructure, lack of funds and unprepared staff, transformation leads to wasted spending and missed results. A successful transformation project changes the business process model and makes the company more efficient. Conclusion A digital transformation project alone doesn't guarantee success. Management must understand at the review stage how realistic the project is and whether the company is ready for it at its current life-cycle stage. But ignoring digitalisation is even more dangerous: technology players take over markets. That's why a comprehensive evaluation method is needed, with non-financial metrics next to financial ones. I now study the same question — "is the company ready, and what should be prepared upfront" — for AI: see the talk on infrastructure requirements and the research page. 📎 Defence slides, PDF (in Russian)

t: Hooked by Nir Eyal: how products become habits
x: Hooked by Nir Eyal: how products become habits Key ideas from the book about products people use out of habit, without ads or reminders: the four steps a habit is built from, and where the line with manipulation lies. Nir Eyal has long worked at the intersection of psychology, technology and business. In the book he describes the Hook model — a cycle the user goes through again and again until the product becomes part of their day. The Hook model: four steps Trigger. First external — a notification, an email, a button. Over time it's replaced by an internal one: boredom, anxiety, the urge to talk to someone. Action. The simplest behaviour done in anticipation of a reward. It happens when motivation, ability and a trigger coincide, so every extra step lowers the chance of action. Variable reward. A reward you can't predict exactly holds attention more strongly. Eyal names three kinds: the tribe (approval from others), the hunt (new information, finds) and the self (mastery, completion). Investment. The user puts something into the product — data, content, followers, settings, reputation. This makes the product more valuable to them and loads the next trigger. When a habit is possible A habit forms when a product is used often and is clearly useful. A rare but very useful behaviour can also become a habit, but it's harder. Ethics Eyal proposes a matrix: would you use the product yourself, and does it materially improve people's lives? Yes and yes — you're a "facilitator". It doesn't improve lives but you use it — an "entertainer". It improves lives but you don't use it — a "peddler". Neither — a "dealer". What a PM can take from it Break the key scenario into the four steps: which internal trigger we serve, how many steps to the action, what varies in the reward, and what the user leaves in the product so they come back. Who should read it PMs of consumer products and anyone working on retention. Read it together with the ethics chapter — the model works equally well for helpful and harmful products.

t: The Goal by Eliyahu Goldratt: the theory of constraints as a novel
x: The Goal by Eliyahu Goldratt: the theory of constraints as a novel Key ideas from a business novel about a plant manager who has three months to save his factory — and about the theory of constraints, which has since been applied far beyond factories. Eliyahu Goldratt was a physicist and the author of the theory of constraints. The Goal is written as a novel: plant manager Alex Rogo talks to his former teacher Jonah, who asks questions instead of giving answers. What a company's goal is The goal is to make money now and in the future. Everything else — machine efficiency, staff utilisation, report quality — is only a means. Goldratt proposes three measures: Throughput — the rate at which the system generates money through sales; Inventory — the money invested in things the system intends to sell; Operating expense — the money spent turning inventory into throughput. The bottleneck decides everything A system's output equals the output of its slowest link. An hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost for the whole system. An hour saved at a non-bottleneck is a mirage. The scout hike scene explains this better than any diagram: the troop moves at the speed of the slowest boy, and the gaps grow because of statistical fluctuations and dependent events. Five focusing steps Identify the system's constraint. Exploit it to the maximum. Subordinate everything else to it. Elevate the constraint. Go back to step one when the constraint moves — and don't let inertia become the new constraint. What a PM can take from it Look for the bottleneck in the delivery process: reviews, testing, approvals, one overloaded role. Speeding up everything else is useless while the bottleneck stays. The same logic applies to a funnel: improve the step where you lose the most users. Who should read it Anyone who manages processes and teams. The novel form makes it an easy read, and its ideas are worth discussing with your engineering team.

t: The Innovator's Dilemma by Clayton Christensen: why strong companies lose to newcomers
x: The Innovator's Dilemma by Clayton Christensen: why strong companies lose to newcomers Key ideas from the book on disruptive innovation: why well-managed companies that do everything right lose their market to simpler, cheaper products. Clayton Christensen was a professor at Harvard Business School. The book came out in 1997 and introduced the term "disruptive innovation". The paradox he describes: market leaders lose not because of bad management but precisely because they follow good management practice. Sustaining and disruptive technologies Sustaining technologies improve the product along the dimensions the best customers already value. Leaders almost always win this race. Disruptive technologies are initially worse on the main dimensions but simpler, cheaper or more convenient. They come in at the low end or create a new market where the old metrics don't matter. Why leaders don't respond The best customers don't ask for a simple, cheap product — they ask for improvements. The new market is too small to move a big company's revenue. Margins are lower, and resources flow to where margins are higher. Meanwhile the disruptive technology improves faster than mainstream needs grow — and one day it becomes "good enough". Christensen shows this with hard disk drives, excavators and steel: each new generation of technology came in from the edge of the market. What to do Put the disruptive project into a separate small team for which a small market is a big success. Expect the first guess about the market to be wrong and plan for cheap attempts. Look for new markets and new customers instead of selling the novelty to current ones. What a PM can take from it Check whether the product is "overshooting" customers with features they no longer need, and watch cheap alternatives that look unserious today. Who should read it PMs and leaders in mature companies — to see threats; and startup founders — to understand a big player's blind spot.

t: Business Model Generation by Osterwalder and Pigneur: a business model on one page
x: Business Model Generation by Osterwalder and Pigneur: a business model on one page Key ideas from the book that gave the world the Business Model Canvas: the nine blocks every business is made of, common patterns, and ways to design new models. Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur wrote the book together with hundreds of practitioners from many countries. The main tool is the Business Model Canvas: one page that shows how a company creates, delivers and captures value. The nine blocks Customer segments — for whom we create value. Value propositions — which customer problems we solve and needs we meet. Channels — how we deliver value to the customer. Customer relationships — how we acquire and retain customers. Revenue streams — what customers pay for and how. Key resources — what the model needs to work. Key activities — what we must do well. Key partnerships — who helps us and what we rely on. Cost structure — what the model costs. The right side of the canvas is about value and the customer; the left side is about efficiency. Common patterns Unbundling a business into customer relationships, product innovation and infrastructure. The long tail — selling many niche products in small volumes. Multi-sided platforms that bring several customer groups together. Free as a business model — freemium, advertising, bait and hook. Open business models , where a company collaborates with outside partners. How to design models The authors suggest working with the canvas like designers: gathering customer insights, ideating, visual thinking, prototyping models, storytelling and playing out future scenarios. What a PM can take from it Fill in the canvas before development: it quickly shows where the model doesn't add up — for example, the value is clear but there's no channel to the customer, or revenue doesn't cover key costs. Who should read it PMs, founders and anyone who defends a new product to the business. The book is almost entirely visual and works well as a reference to come back to.

t: The Mom Test by Rob Fitzpatrick: how to talk to users so they don't lie to you
x: The Mom Test by Rob Fitzpatrick: how to talk to users so they don't lie to you Key ideas from a short book on customer development: why users politely tell us what we want to hear, and how to ask questions nobody can lie about. The title refers to a simple test: if you ask your mom whether your idea is good, she'll say yes because she loves you. Rob Fitzpatrick shows that almost every interviewee behaves the same way. The problem isn't people, it's the questions. Three rules of a good question Talk about their life, not your idea. Once you pitch the idea, the other person starts judging it — and sparing your feelings. Ask about specifics in the past, not opinions about the future. "When did this last happen? What did you do?" instead of "Would you use this?". Talk less, listen more. An interview isn't a pitch. Three kinds of bad data Compliments — "Great idea!" is worth nothing. Fluff — "I usually", "I would", "someday" are promises, not facts. Ideas and feature requests — behind a request, find the motivation: why the person needs it and what they do today. Commitments instead of promises A good meeting ends with the other person risking something: time (a next meeting, a trial), reputation (an introduction to their boss) or money (a pre-order, a pilot). If all you get is "keep me posted", it's a polite no. How to prepare Write down the three big questions whose answers would change your decisions. Narrow the segment: while it's unclear whom to ask, answers will contradict each other. Keep the conversation casual and write down exact quotes, not your conclusions. What a PM can take from it Before every customer interview, run your questions through the "mom test": can this be answered out of politeness? If so, rephrase it into a question about past behaviour. Who should read it Anyone who interviews users — especially before their first round of customer development. It takes an evening to read and saves months of building things nobody needs.
